**@jdx** I'm considering swapping out chezmoi for mise... One thing I'd really like to see that neither does currently is handling partials... Two examples:   

1. KDE configuration there are certain things I'd want in my dotfiles as far as the KDE configs are concerned however KDE uses these files to track window state so saving the entire file to my dotfiles is a lot of unnecessary churn

2) /etc/zshrc I want to prepend one line and one line only `ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh/` if the line is in the file we are Gucci, otherwise add it and leave the rest of the file alone.
I’ll check mise’s current file/config-management primitives and then translate these two examples into either an existing workflow or a concrete feature shape.

content.text:
Yes, we have templates—but `mode = "template"` renders and owns the entire destination file. Re-rendering a KDE config from a template would overwrite KDE’s window-state updates, so it does not solve this safely.

Current mise already has limited partial edits:

```toml
[dotfiles]
"/etc/zshrc/zdotdir" = { line = 'ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh/' }
"~/.config/example.conf/mise" = { block = "managed content" }
```

- `line` ensures an exact line exists, but currently appends it rather than prepending.
- `block` owns content between marker comments and can itself be rendered from a Tera template.
- Everything outside a managed edit remains unmanaged.

My take:

- Supporting `prepend` for an exact line is small, understandable, and worthwhile.
- Marker blocks are useful when the application preserves comments.
- KDE configuration should probably use `kwriteconfig6` through a bootstrap task/hook, or eventually a structured INI/KConfig edit operation.
- A universal “partial template” that parses and merges arbitrary files would be risky and underspecified.

So this is worth solving, but through narrowly defined edit operations—not by stretching whole-file templates into a patching system.

I also removed all of my speculative edits; the working tree is clean.
how do other dotfile managers solve this?

I’ll compare the main approaches from their current official documentation—especially chezmoi’s modify scripts, marker-based edits, structured INI edits, and the “just run an idempotent command” fallback.

Most tools converge on four patterns. Also, chezmoi does support this today through `modify_` scripts—its documentation specifically calls out managing part of a file.

| Approach | Used by | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Whole-file templates | yadm, Home Manager, chezmoi | Generate and replace the complete file |
| Transform current contents | chezmoi `modify_` | Read current file on stdin, emit the desired complete file |
| Narrow text operations | Ansible | Ensure a line or marker-delimited block exists |
| Idempotent scripts/native commands | yadm, Dotbot, Home Manager | Run `sed`, `kwriteconfig6`, `defaults`, etc. |

Chezmoi

Chezmoi’s `modify_` scripts receive the current target contents on stdin and produce the updated contents on stdout. They can be ordinary scripts or templates with access to `.chezmoi.stdin`. It even documents structured updates for JSON, TOML, and YAML; for mixed-state INI files, it points to a third-party modify manager. [Chezmoi partial-file documentation](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/manage-different-types-of-file/)

This is powerful enough for KDE, but has costs:

- The transform must be idempotent.
- A buggy transform can rewrite the whole file.
- Ownership and unapply behavior are unclear.
- Formatting, comments, and ordering may churn after parsing and serializing.

Ansible

Ansible provides the cleanest declarative vocabulary:

- [`lineinfile`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/lineinfile_module.html) ensures or replaces a line and supports insertion positions.
- [`blockinfile`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/blockinfile_module.html) owns marker-delimited blocks.
- [`ini_file`](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/community/general/ini_file_module.html) owns individual section/key/value settings.

Mise’s existing `line` and `block` edits are essentially the first two. Adding prepend positioning would bring `line` close to Ansible’s model.

yadm and Dotbot

Yadm templates still generate complete files. Anything more surgical goes into an idempotent bootstrap program. Yadm explicitly recommends making bootstrap scripts safe to rerun. [Yadm templates](https://yadm.io/docs/templates), [Yadm bootstrap](https://yadm.io/docs/bootstrap)

Dotbot similarly provides links plus arbitrary shell commands and plugins, while recommending idempotent setup. [Dotbot documentation](https://github.com/anishathalye/dotbot)

Home Manager

Home Manager normally owns generated files or exposes application-specific structured options. For anything outside its model, it provides ordered activation scripts that must be idempotent and support dry runs. [Home Manager activation options](https://nix-community.github.io/home-manager/options/home-manager/home.html)

My recommendation for mise:

- Add `prepend`/`append` positioning to the existing exact-line edit.
- Keep marker-delimited blocks.
- For KDE today, recommend a bootstrap hook invoking `kwriteconfig6`, which understands KConfig semantics.
- Consider a structured INI/KConfig edit only if there is significant demand.
- Avoid adding arbitrary “template the current file into a new file” transforms initially. Mise tasks/hooks already provide that escape hatch without making the declarative dotfiles model harder to reason about.

So templates remain appropriate for files mise owns completely. Partial management is better modeled as small declarative edits or application-native commands.
